title: Weekly links October 23: macro impacts of migration on poverty, big African cities and jobs, how to read a paper, and more…
gist: A weekly roundup of development-economics links: Nepal's labor-export route out of poverty, a counterfactual-minded take on African urbanization, LLM performance on econometric coding tasks, and an Ethiopian vacancy-subsidy experiment.

insights.claim: Nepal cut extreme poverty from seven in ten people in 1995 to fewer than one in 40 by 2022, a pace matched only by China, driven by labor export rather than factories or foreign investment.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Remittance-led poverty reduction is an alternative path that matters for remittance-dependent economies.
insights.quote: Nepal’s escape from extreme poverty was built not on factories or foreign investment but on the export of labor.

insights.claim: African cities expanded by 15 million people annually recently and are expected to grow by 19 million annually by 2050, over 50,000 new city dwellers a day, with a lack of infrastructure and formal jobs.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Urban growth outpacing infrastructure and formal jobs is a stability and demand-side question.

insights.claim: Critiques of African urbanization often ignore the counterfactual; a UN report covering 2,600 cities in 34 countries finds African cities outperform their national averages and kept performance while growing by 500 million people.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Challenges the narrative of urban growth as pure poverty trap; ask 'better compared to what'.

insights.claim: In a benchmark of 40 econometric tasks, letting LLMs run and revise their code raised correct results from 79 percent to 97 percent, but remaining failures are scripts that run without errors yet return wrong numbers.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Agentic code execution greatly improves quantitative-analysis reliability, but silent errors keep human verification essential.

insights.claim: An Ethiopian experiment subsidizing formal vacancy postings led SMEs to post more white-collar vacancies but not to hire more, possibly because firms learned the wages required to fill the positions.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Search-cost subsidies may not raise hiring if wage expectations are the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Reading a paper by asking what its contribution and gap are, rather than only its identification and result, helps find the next research step.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Minor methodological tip for research practice.
